content.text: 1.2.4 Captions (Live)
Learning objectives
Recognize live synchronized media, plan captions for its audio, and explain how live captions differ from captions prepared for a recording. This is a Level AA criterion.
Access during a live event

Live captions communicate the words and meaningful sounds of an event while it happens. During a streamed lecture, a deaf attendee may need the presenter's explanation and audience questions in text at the time of the discussion, rather than after the event. The criterion applies to live audio content in synchronized media, such as audio and video presented together as the event occurs. WCAG's definition also covers audio or video synchronized with another format or time-based interactive components, subject to its defined exception for clearly labeled media alternatives for text. Live audio-only content is addressed separately by 1.2.9.

Captions should convey the relevant audio, including speakers and meaningful sounds when needed to follow the event. The event is not fully accessible simply because a caption button exists; the caption stream must actually communicate what is happening.
Plan and test the workflow

Choose a captioning arrangement appropriate to the event and its languages. Provide captioners with agendas, terminology, and speaker names in advance where possible. Test the audio feed, player, caption display, and handoff between speakers before the event. Ask speakers to use microphones and identify themselves where that makes the discussion easier to follow. Arrange a way to respond if captions stop during the event.

For example, an online panel shows the host's captions but omits audience questions because the question microphone is not included in the captioning feed. Include all relevant audio in that feed and test an audience question before starting. Automated output can make errors with names, accents, overlapping voices, or technical terms, so evaluate the actual result rather than assuming its accuracy.
Recordings and other criteria

A transcript published the next day does not provide access to the live discussion. If the event is later offered as a recording, assess the prerecorded version against the applicable prerecorded-media criteria, including 1.2.2 and the requirements for visual information. Captions address audio content; visual-only instructions may require separate access.
Worked example: a live class

A lecturer and a remote guest present a lesson and students submit spoken questions. The captioner receives the lecturer's microphone but not the remote guest's audio. The page displays captions, yet the guest's explanation and questions are absent. This creates gaps in the actual lecture, even though the caption feature appears to be working.

Before the event, route each relevant source to the captioning workflow. Test a guest contribution and a student question, not just the host's greeting. Supply subject terms and the correct spelling of names to the caption provider. During the event, designate a person to monitor the caption output and a way for attendees to report a failure. If a feed stops, address the interruption and communicate with participants using an accessible channel.
Evaluate the result

Compare the caption stream with the live event: are changes of speaker clear where needed, are questions and answers present, and do important sound cues appear? If automated captions misidentify a technical term or drop an overlapping speaker, investigate the workflow and correct the problem where possible. Planning improves the likelihood of useful captions, but the actual output and its availability are what learners experience. Afterward, review the recording independently because its applicable requirements differ.
Handling an interruption in practice

Imagine the caption feed freezes halfway through a public meeting. The audio continues and a vote is announced. Users who depend on captions miss the discussion and decision. A useful event plan identifies who notices the failure, how the host is alerted, and how attendees are informed. Depending on the circumstances, the host may pause the meeting while the caption feed is restored and repeat information missed during the interruption. Planning a response does not guarantee that every event will run perfectly, but it gives the team a concrete path to restore access.

Before the next event, review what failed. Did the captioner lose the audio feed? Was the player displaying stale captions? Did an audience microphone bypass the system? Reproduce the issue in a test, correct the routing or configuration, and verify the result from a participant's view. Ask a tester to join with captions enabled rather than relying only on the host's control panel.

Live output can contain technical vocabulary that an automatic tool mishears. Provide names and terminology in advance, speak clearly into microphones, and avoid overlapping speakers where possible. These are production practices rather than substitutes for the criterion: the purpose is for the actual live audio information to be conveyed to users through captions. When a recording is published later, review and correct the prerecorded captions separately.
Required lesson activity

Create a live-caption plan for a panel with a host, two guests, and audience questions. Identify the audio feeds, preparation material, pre-event checks, and steps to take if captions fail. Explain how you will verify that audience questions are represented.
